summary: The product of a design team in the Traffic Engineering Working Group that collected requirements for network hierarchy and survivability in service provider networks. It adds expanded definitions and suggests a small set of interoperable survivability approaches.

plainLanguage.summary: If one road is broken, traffic should reroute. This document lists the requirements for networks with several layers, so each layer can recover without confusing the others.

questions: how do network layers recover from failures
what is the difference between protection and restoration
what is a shared risk group
what is a hold off timer in multilayer recovery
subtitle: A design team's list of what service providers needed for recovering from failures across network layers and areas.

tldr.problem: Service providers run networks made of several technology layers and routing areas, and had no small, agreed set of interoperable ways to survive a failure such as a cut fiber.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines survivability and hierarchy terms, proposes four initial mechanisms (two kinds of 1:1 path protection, local restoration and path restoration) with timing bounds, and asks for loose coordination between layers using hold-off timers.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol: it was meant to focus the work of the TEWG and CCAMP working groups and says survivability schemes can be concatenated across hierarchy boundaries.

today: RFC 3386 is an Informational document from November 2002 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records requirements rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
RFC 3386 is the output of the Network Hierarchy and Survivability Techniques Design Team, set up within the Traffic Engineering Working Group. The team collected the near-term, practical requirements for survivability and hierarchy in service provider networks.

Its conclusion is that a small set of interoperable survivability approaches is needed for packet and non-packet networks, and that they operate primarily at a single network layer. For hierarchy, the team saw no near-term need for direct signaling between layers. The pressing need was to set up many Label Switched Paths (LSPs) across a network that uses a hierarchical IGP, to support layer 2 and layer 3 VPN services.

The initial focus is intra-domain operation. Rules at domain boundaries are raised but not treated in depth.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of network experts wrote down what big network companies really need so that equipment from different makers can recover from breakages in the same way.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Hierarchy
sections.content:
Hierarchy is an abstraction technique for building large systems. The RFC looks at it two ways.

  • Vertical hierarchy is between technology layers, such as optical, SDH/SONET, ATM, MPLS and IP. Each layer has its own survivability: for example SDH/SONET has automatic protection switching, while IP restores service by rerouting after routing convergence, which may take a few seconds to several minutes.
  • Horizontal hierarchy is between areas or administrative subdivisions within one layer, such as BGP confederations, separate Autonomous Systems or multi-area OSPF.

The RFC also defines the vocabulary used later: a working entity carries traffic normally, a protection entity takes over when it fails, and a shared risk group (SRG) is a set of network elements hit by the same fault, such as links sharing one conduit.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks are stacked like floors of a building, and some are split like neighborhoods in a town. Each needs its own plan for when something breaks.

sections.title: The Four Initial Survivability Mechanisms
sections.content:
The scope is deliberately narrow: the RFC addresses only backhoe failures in the inter-office connections of a provider network. Linecard and node failures can be treated as sets of link failures. Control-plane failures, configuration errors, security breaches and congestion are out of scope.

It then asks for four mechanisms.

  • 1:1 path protection with pre-established capacity. The head end sets up a protection connection that is failure-disjoint from the working one, using SRG information. Traffic normally flows only on the working connection.
  • 1:1 path protection with pre-planned capacity. The protection connection is also pre-signaled, but its capacity can be shared (double-booked) between SRG-disjoint failures. This uses resources better but needs more careful planning.
  • Local restoration. Connectivity is repaired close to the fault, because signaling a whole new path takes too long. Head ends must be able to opt connections in or out, and later re-groom paths since the repair may be suboptimal.
  • Path restoration. The originating element reroutes after being told of the failure. It needs no new mechanism, is efficient with resources, and is slower.

The RFC suggests initial deployment of 1:1 path protection with pre-established capacity plus local restoration.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to detour around a broken road: have a spare road ready, have a shared spare road, fix the road right where it broke, or let the driver plan a new route from the start.

sections.title: Timing Bounds and Priorities
sections.content:
Different applications tolerate different outages. Best-effort data can simply be rerouted at the IP layer. Premium data must meet TCP timeout or application timer requirements. For voice, call cutoff is in the range of 140 msec to 2 sec. Mission-critical applications cannot tolerate even brief interruptions.

The RFC proposes timing bounds for each mechanism, all exclusive of signal propagation (see the table). It admits that nobody on the team would attest to the scientific merit of these bounds for any specific application.

Because restoration is slower and more variable than protection, restoration priority must be implemented to decide the order in which connections are restored. Preemption priority is used only when not all connections can be restored, releasing those with lower preemption priority.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone call hangs up if the line is silent too long, so the fastest fixes are saved for the things that cannot wait. The most important traffic gets fixed first.

sections.title: Layers, Timers and Area Boundaries
sections.content:
When several layers can each recover from a fault, they may all react at once. The RFC's default answer is nested timers: a lower layer that recovers more slowly causes a hold-off timer to delay the higher layer. For example, MPLS recovery waits until SDH/SONET protection switching has had time to act. The price is a longer overall recovery, and a race condition if the timers are set badly.

If the lower layer cannot recover (an unprotected SDH/SONET linear circuit, say), it must be able to tell the higher layer at once. Faults at higher layers should not trigger actions at lower layers.

For horizontal hierarchy, the main driver is edge-to-edge signaling for layer 2 and layer 3 VPNs across a multi-area OSPF or multi-level IS-IS network. The RFC says multi-area traffic engineering requirements need to be developed. For survivability across an area boundary, it finds it sufficient to concatenate schemes that are each protected within their own area, for example joined at an OSPF ABR, though that router is then a common point of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: If two helpers both try to fix the same broken pipe at once, they get in each other's way. So the upstairs helper waits a moment to let the downstairs helper try first.

sections.title: Protecting Shared Risk Group Data
sections.content:
The set of SRGs defined for a network, and which nodes and links belong to each, is sensitive information. An adversary who learned it could design an attack and maximize its effect.

The RFC therefore asks that SRG labels be encoded so that physical location, function, purpose, customer or fault type cannot be easily read, and that SRG information carried in the control and management plane can be encrypted. IPsec on all packets carrying SRG information is given as an example approach.
sections.plainLanguage: A map showing exactly where a town's bridges are weak would help a troublemaker, so the map has to be kept secret.
